title: Limitations of the Central Limit Theorem with small sample size and skewed population
scenario_markdown: An insurance analytics group models commercial flood damage claims. The population distribution of individual claims is heavily right-skewed with extreme positive outliers ($	ext{mean } \mu = \$25,000, \text{standard deviation } \sigma = \$18,000$). An intern takes a small random sample of $n = 9$ claims and uses the standard normal distribution ($Z$-table) to calculate the probability that the sample mean exceeds $\$30,000$, claiming that 'by the Central Limit Theorem, sample averages are always normally distributed.'
assumptions: Commercial flood claims follow a heavily right-skewed, non-normal distribution
No population normality can be assumed
source_refs: Course Module 4: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual limitations of CLT: n = 9 is insufficient for non-normal populations; CLT requires n >= 30 when population is skewed. If population is normal, X_bar is normal for any n.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the primary statistical flaw in the intern's justification for using the normal distribution?

options.text_markdown: The Central Limit Theorem requires a sufficiently large sample size (typically $n \ge 30$) when the population is non-normal. With only $n = 9$ from a heavily skewed population, the sampling distribution of $ ar{X}$ remains skewed.
The Central Limit Theorem applies exclusively to discrete counts, not continuous monetary values.
options.hint_markdown: The CLT applies to both discrete and continuous random variables with finite variance; it is not restricted to counts.

options.text_markdown: The normal approximation requires a sample size of at least $n \ge 1{,}000$ before any sampling distribution can be analyzed.
options.hint_markdown: The standard introductory textbook rule of thumb for the Central Limit Theorem is $n \ge 30$, not thousands.

stages.explanation_markdown: The Central Limit Theorem is an asymptotic theorem: as sample size increases, the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ approaches a normal distribution. When the population distribution is severely skewed, small samples ($n = 9$) do not provide enough averaging to smooth out the skewness. The textbook rule of thumb requires $n \ge 30$ before assuming approximate normality for non-normal populations.

stages.prompt_markdown: Under what condition WOULD a sample of size $n = 9$ yield an exactly normal sampling distribution for the sample mean $\bar{X}$?

options.text_markdown: If the underlying population of claim amounts itself is normally distributed.
If the sample mean is confirmed to equal the sample median in the 9 observed claims.
options.hint_markdown: Even if sample mean and median happen to coincide in one small sample, that does not guarantee that the sampling distribution across all possible samples is normal.

options.text_markdown: If the finite population correction factor is applied to reduce the standard error.
options.hint_markdown: The finite population correction modifies the standard error formula when sampling from a finite population; it has no effect on whether the distribution shape is normal.

stages.explanation_markdown: If the population itself is normally distributed $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, then the linear combination $\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i$ is exactly normally distributed for ANY sample size $n$, even $n = 2$ or $n = 9$. When the population is not normal, we must rely on the CLT and have $n \ge 30$.

stages.prompt_markdown: How does using the symmetric standard normal distribution table affect the intern's calculation of the upper tail probability $P(\bar{X} > \$30,000)$ on this right-skewed data with $n = 9$?

options.text_markdown: Because the true sampling distribution retains substantial right-skewness, the right tail is fatter and more elongated than the normal curve, causing the normal table to underestimate the true probability of high claim averages.
The expected value $E[\bar{X}]$ will no longer equal the population mean $\mu = \$25,000$.
options.hint_markdown: The sample mean remains an unbiased estimator ($E[\bar{X}] = \mu$) regardless of population shape or sample size; skewness alters the shape of the sampling distribution, not its center.

options.text_markdown: The sampling distribution collapses into a uniform rectangular distribution between $\$0$ and $\$50,000$.
options.hint_markdown: Averages of skewed random variables retain skewness; they do not flatten into a uniform distribution.

stages.explanation_markdown: Right-skewed distributions have heavy upper tails and frequent positive outliers. When $n$ is small ($n = 9$), averaging does not fully eliminate this skewness. Consequently, extreme positive sample averages occur more frequently than predicted by a thin-tailed, symmetric bell curve, so a standard normal calculation underestimates the upper-tail probability.
